catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Phonological divergence (synchronic)' (pp. 29-42): p. 31, the vowel-length/stress statement; pp. 41-42, lexical fixing of penultimate length and the morphophonemic length shifts. page numbers read from the page headers; the scan's garbles them ('52', 'k2'), the origin of the earlier 'p. 51 / p. 61' locators.
catalog_quote: Vowel length is distinctive in all Bikol area dialects, but stress, or loudness, is not. Distinctive vowel length may occur between any vowel other than the final vowel of a word and a single consonant; e.g. Leg sa:lug 'river' (cf. salug 'floor'); ma:ba:sa 'will read' (cf. maba:sa 'able to be read'). Length is non-distinctive after the final vowel of a word. In inherited words, length does not occur before a consonant cluster. In borrowed words, however, length does occur before clusters: Leg pi:dru 'Pedro'; gu:stu 'want, like' (from Sp. gusto). [printed p. 31] ... Basic vowel length within a root is fixed arbitrarily in the lexicon. That is, in its basic lexical form, a root has either a long or short penultimate vowel. Thus there are minimal pairs such as Leg salug 'floor', sa:lug 'river'. There are a number of morphophonemic alternations involving the shift of vowel length. That is, in certain inflected and derived forms, vowel length may appear on a different vowel of the root from the one on which it appears in the lexical form of the root. For example, with most verbal suffixes vowel length appears on the final vowel of any root having penultimate vowel length lexically: basa:hun 'to be read' (ba:sa 'to read'); taba:ŋan 'to be helped' (ta:baŋ 'to help'). Otherwise length does not appear: darahun 'to be carried' (dara 'to carry'); marumduman 'to be remembered' (rumdum 'to remember'). [printed pp. 41-42]

new_statements.rule_in_words: No distinctive stress in the sense of loudness; instead every root carries a lexically arbitrary long or short penultimate vowel (the Philippine accent contrast), so accent placement is unpredictable from the segmental shape and must be listed per root; suffixation shifts the length rightward and some affixes impose penult length.
new_statements.exceptions: Length occurs before consonant clusters only in loans (pi:dru, gu:stu); length after the final vowel of a word is non-distinctive; lexically fixed length shifts under suffixation (p. 61-62). Lobel 2013: fn. 3 p. 287 warns that some Bikol subgroup members have lost contrastive stress (Lobel 2003 on Rinconada), so individual Inland varieties may differ; Olson et al. 2009's Buhi'non list shows mostly final stress in citation forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation/lexical forms; the statement is made once for 'all Bikol area dialects' (the eleven dialects surveyed, including the Inland dialects Daraga, Oas, Libon and Buhi that make up alba1269), and the illustrative forms are Legazpi (Coastal Bikol). McFarland explicitly denies distinctive stress (loudness) and locates the contrast in vowel length; this is the ordinary Philippine 'accent' contrast (long penult = penult accent vs short penult = final accent), which is why the reading is lexical (unpredictable) rather than no word stress according to the source. Morphophonemics: with most verbal suffixes the length moves to the root-final vowel (basa:hun); certain affixes impose penult length regardless of the root (paraqu:ma, paraba:sa); length never precedes a consonant cluster in inherited words.
new_statements.identity_note: McFarland 1974 is a survey of eleven Bikol-area dialects; the deciding statement is made for 'all Bikol area dialects' and the examples are Legazpi (Coastal Bikol, cent2087). Of his Inland dialects, Daraga and Oas (= Miraya/West Albay), Libon and Buhi belong to alba1269, while Iriga is Rinconada (irig1242). No opened source gives a stress rule for one alba1269 variety alone; the Buhi'non wordlist (Olson et al. 2009, Buhi, Camarines Sur; ABVD glottocode buhi1243) is corpus evidence only. Wikipedia's claim that Albay Bikol 'lacks stressed syllables' is unsourced and contradicted by the wordlist and Lobel 2005 accent marks. Fincke 2002 (Sto. Domingo, Albay) is linked by Glottolog to alba1269 but Sto. Domingo is a coastal town, so that link is doubtful.

new_statements.quote: The varieties of WAB, together with certain other language areas within the Bikol region, lost the historical vowel length distinction on the penultimate syllable of roots. Thus, a reconstructed form such as *saːbi ‘say’ becomes /saːbi/ in Tagalog and most other Central Philippine languages but /sabi/ in WAB. Like other Central Philippine languages, words with a short penult obtain prominence on the final syllable from the phrase level (Kaufman and Himmelmann, 2024). Vowel length is reintroduced through the morphology, where it still plays a role in aspect inflection, and through the synchronic deletion of glottal stop and historical loss of *h.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's existing statement (McFarland 1974, p. 31: 'Vowel length is distinctive in all Bikol area dialects, but stress, or loudness, is not'; his Table 1 marks vowel length distinctive in every inventory incl. Libon, Iriga, Buhi; reading lexical (unpredictable)) treats the whole Inland group as having lexically contrastive penult length. Borja 2024 agrees that loudness-stress is not the contrast but states that the West Albay varieties (Polangui/Balugo) have LOST root vowel length, leaving only phrase-level final-syllable prominence plus morphological length -- i.e. no lexical accent contrast in roots, a different type from 'lexical'. The difference is variety-conditioned: Borja notes…
new_statements.rule_in_words: West Albay Bikol (Polangui and Balugo) has lost the inherited lexical vowel-length (penult long vs short) contrast in roots (*Vː > V, Table 2.3), so roots carry no lexical accent; every root, having a short penult, receives prominence on its final syllable, assigned at the phrase level (following Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024). Vowel length survives only as a morphological exponent (imperfective: CVː- reduplication, ná-/naká- progressive vs na-/naka- perfective, Tables 3.4-3.6; acute accent in the practical orthography = length, Table 3.3) and as compensatory/coalescence length from glottal-stop deletion and *h loss (kaɨn -> [kɨːn], daun -> [doːn]). In Table 2.4 the Naga Bikol cognates are written with acute accents (penult length) while the Balugo forms carry none, consistent with the loss.
new_statements.exceptions: Length reappears (i) morphologically in aspect inflection (vowel length on the prefix or CVː reduplication marks imperfective) and (ii) phonetically through vowel coalescence after loss of intervocalic glottal stop / *h in casual speech; loanwords not discussed for prosody. No statement that any WAB roots retain lexical length.
new_statements.identity_note: Borja 2024 describes West Albay Bikol (WAB, ISO 639-3 fbl) as spoken in Polangui town and its barangay Balugo (Albay), documented from diaspora speakers in New York (author's family); Glottolog folds fbl together with Buhi'non (ubl), Libon (lbl) and Miraya (rbl) into alba1269. The catalog's McFarland-based statement covers the whole Inland group with examples mostly from Legazpi and WAB data mainly from Oas. A variety-level note for fbl/West Albay (no lexical length; phrase-final prominence per Borja 2024) would resolve the apparent conflict without changing the aggregate's McFarland-based reading for Buhi-non/Libon/Oas.

readall_conflicts: McFarland 1974 (catalog's existing statement) says vowel length is lexically distinctive on the penult in all Bikol area dialects, including the Inland towns (Oas, Libon, Iriga, Buhi, Daraga), with loudness-stress non-distinctive -> lexical (unpredictable). Borja 2024 says the West Albay Bikol varieties of Polangui and Balugo (ISO fbl, one of the four codes merged into alba1269) have lost the root vowel-length contrast entirely (*Vː > V), so roots have no lexical accent and prominence falls on the word-final syllable from the phrase level (Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024), with length surviving only as an aspect exponent (ná- vs na-, CVː- reduplication) and from glottal/h loss -> phrase-level prominence only for WAB. The two agree that intensity-stress is not contrastive; they disagree on whether lexical length/accent exists, and the disagreement lines up with variety (McFarland's WAB data = Oas, 1970s; Borja = Polangui/Balugo diaspora speakers, 2024) rather than with analysis. Buhi'non materials held by the project (Olson, Ballenas & Borromeo 2009 wordlist; Lobel 2005) still show both penult and final accent, siding with McFarland for that component.

tone.quote: Phonetic rules. These rules have generated the correct placement of accents. It only remains to produce the phonetics. Accented vowels are high-pitched, long, and stressed in contrast to unaccented vowels. If two accented vowels occur in the same word, the first has these characteristics to a greater degree than the second. An accentless phrase is stressed on its final syllable. In addition, closed syllables optionally have stress, though it is weaker than that on an accented syllable in the same phrase.
